strengths: MSAM offers a simple, practically useful way to reuse momentum for parameter perturbations with one forward/backward pass per update. The efficient implementation and reported relative speed of 0.99 support the claim of negligible overhead over the base optimizer.

The experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over SGD/AdamW across CNNs and vision transformers. For example, CIFAR100 WRN-16-4 improves from 76.90% to 79.11%. The comparisons with efficient SAM variants, compatibility with adaptive and BN-only perturbations, and equal-compute experiments strengthen the practical contribution.

The extensive ablations provide useful insights beyond the optimizer itself. In particular, Appendix A.2 identifies the importance of decoupling perturbation magnitude from the learning-rate schedule, while the momentum-direction analyses help explain why negative perturbations can increase loss. The observation that lower measured sharpness does not necessarily yield better accuracy is also valuable.

The manuscript provides training configurations, full perturbation-strength sweeps, and a code link. It openly discusses instability, larger-model performance gaps, and limited ImageNet repetitions; this transparency supports reproducibility and helps delimit the findings.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Appendix A.1 is incorrect as stated. Proposition 1 fails for negative-trace Hessians: with H = -I, its left side is -E[||epsilon||² 1{||epsilon|| <= rho}], which is strictly greater than the claimed upper bound -rho². Setting 1 does not generally exclude negative trace. Theorem 3 also does not state or justify the assumptions needed to transfer a PAC-Bayes bound on randomized weights to the deterministic population loss. Consequently, Section 4.1's claim that improved generalization directly follows from this analysis is unsupported.

The ImageNet comparison does not apply equally favorable warm-up settings. MSAM perturbations are disabled during warm-up, whereas SAM remains active, despite Table A.2 showing that disabling SAM during warm-up improves accuracy from 69.2% to 69.8%, versus MSAM's 69.1%. Claims of comparable accuracy also need qualification: Table 2 shows deficits of 2.4 percentage points for ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs and 2.0 points for ViT-B/16. Matched warm-up and compute comparisons on these configurations would better establish the tradeoff.

The model-selection protocol is insufficiently specified. Appendix A.15 reports the best perturbation strengths alongside test-accuracy sweeps, without describing an independent validation split or selection rule. This leaves potential test-set selection bias unresolved. Moreover, variability measured from baseline runs on the smallest ImageNet models cannot establish uncertainty for other optimizers and architectures, particularly when interpreting the small ResNet gains.

The gradient-similarity diagnostic in Section 4.2 discards potentially important information. A zero angle after projecting the MSAM gradient onto the SAM/SGD plane can coexist with a large orthogonal residual, so it does not demonstrate closeness of the actual update directions. Full-vector similarities and residual magnitudes are needed to substantiate this interpretation. The curvature and feature-rank observations likewise do not establish a causal explanation for generalization.

Some supporting material remains incomplete. Algorithm 1 initializes the momentum to zero but divides by its norm without specifying a guard. Appendix A.16 leaves attack citations unresolved and reports 'default hyperparameters' without sufficient attack settings for reproduction. These are secondary concerns, but they weaken the manuscript's clarity and completeness.
